What is the general limitation period for an obligation in the Civil Code (fifteen years), and which text sets it?
Which shorter limitation periods apply to periodic payments (rent, interest, wages, maintenance arrears, other periodic dues: five years), and are they lost even if the debtor acknowledges them?
Which short limitation periods apply to the rights of professionals (doctors, lawyers, engineers, experts, bailiffs, teachers) and from what event do they run?

Which one-year limitations apply (merchants and manufacturers for goods supplied to non-merchants, hotel and restaurant keepers, workers' and servants' wages and supplies), and is the debtor who invokes them bound to take an oath that he paid?
How is a limitation period counted: by days, not hours; is the first day excluded; does the period end at the end of its last day?

From what event does limitation start: the day the debt becomes due; for a conditional debt, the day the condition is met; for a debt with a term, the day the term arrives; for a guarantee claim, the day eviction occurs?
When the due date depends on the creditor's will, when does limitation start?

What suspends limitation: a legal or material impediment that prevents the creditor from claiming (force majeure), incapacity without a legal representative, relations between spouses, principal and representative?
Does suspension apply to the five-year and shorter periods with respect to persons lacking capacity?

What interrupts limitation: a judicial claim, even before a court without jurisdiction; a payment order request; a seizure; the debtor's declaration in bankruptcy; a step taken by the creditor in a pending proceeding?
Does a claim later dismissed, withdrawn or annulled for a defect of form, or a proceeding that lapses, still interrupt limitation?
Does the debtor's acknowledgment, express or implied, interrupt limitation, and does a pledge left with the creditor count as implied acknowledgment?
After interruption, what new period runs, and from when; when does the new period become fifteen years (judgment, acknowledgment of a short-period debt)?
Who may raise limitation: the debtor, his creditors, any interested person; may it be raised at any stage of the proceedings, including on appeal?
Does the court raise limitation of its own motion? (Expected answer: no, it must be pleaded.)
May a party waive limitation before it has run; may it waive acquired limitation; may parties agree to a period different from the statutory one?
Does limitation of the principal right extinguish accessories (interest) even if their own period has not run?
Limitation for the claim for compensation arising from a harmful act (tort): fifteen years from the harmful act, and the text that sets it.
Limitation of the action for annulment of a voidable contract and of the action for absolute nullity (fifteen years from the contract).

Short periods inside specific contracts: latent defects in sale (one year from delivery), lesion in sale of real property, guarantee of contractors and architects (decennial), and whether they are limitation or forfeiture.

Forfeiture (سقوط) versus limitation (تقادم): forfeiture periods are not suspended or interrupted in principle and the court may raise them of its own motion when of public order; how to tell which one a text sets.
Counting of procedural periods (CPCA): the day of service and the day of expiry are not counted; full days; a period ending on a public holiday or weekend day is extended to the next working day.
Are procedural periods extended for a party who lives abroad (distance period), and by how much?
Which procedural periods in CPCA are sanctioned by forfeiture of the right to act (appeal, opposition, cassation periods) and does the court raise the expiry of a period of its own motion?

Inadmissibility pleas (CPCA): limitation, forfeiture, res judicata, lack of standing or interest are grounds of inadmissibility; may they be raised at any stage; must the court raise those of public order of its own motion?

Labour claims: the claim must be filed within six months of the delivery of the non-conciliation record, under penalty of forfeiture (CPCA on social matters); how is that six-month period counted under the procedural counting rule?
Labour claims: the exemptions from prior conciliation (employer bankrupt or in judicial settlement, employer abroad, public servants) and how they affect the starting event of the six-month period.
Wages: which limitation period applies to arrears of wages (periodic payment five years under the Civil Code, or a one-year period for workers' wages), and is there a special labour-law text?
Does a formal notice (إعذار) interrupt limitation? (From memory: no, only a judicial claim or acknowledgment does.)
Does the State or a public body get any special limitation regime, and are actions against the administration subject to different periods before the administrative courts?
Commercial matters: is there a shorter limitation for commercial obligations or bills of exchange, and is it in the Commercial Code?
Commercial leases: periods for the renewal claim and the eviction compensation claim (two years) under the Commercial Code — limitation or forfeiture?
Family matters: periods relevant to maintenance arrears and to claims after divorce; does the family code set any forfeiture?
Real property: acquisitive prescription periods (fifteen years, ten years with good faith and title) are a different institution from extinctive limitation and must not be confused with it.
What the lawyer must state in the petition to anticipate a limitation plea: the due date, any interruption (acknowledgment, prior claim), any suspension.
Amendments: CPCA 08-09 replaced the old Code of Civil Procedure in 2009; the Civil Code amendments of 2005 touched formal notice and default but, as far as I remember, not the limitation articles.
